title: Backups, snapshots, forks and undo
standfirst: Four different jobs hide under “snapshot”: a restore point on one machine, a reusable image for new machines, a copy of a running machine, and a backup that survives losing the host. Ask which one you are getting.

concept.heading: The four jobs
paragraphs: A restore point lets you rewind one machine after a bad change. A reusable image lets you start many identical machines from a known-good setup. A fork copies a machine, ideally while it is running, so you can try something without risking the original. A backup survives losing the host or the account.

Providers rarely offer all four, and the same word covers different subsets. Agent 37 has no snapshot product at all: it has a sleep checkpoint (not cloneable), a folder-scoped backup, and Dockerfile-built templates. Boat has automatic disk snapshots every minute but only the newest is usable, plus named saved snapshots that never expire. InstaBox's snapshot is disk-only and may stop the machine to take it.

concept.heading: Memory is the dividing line
paragraphs: A snapshot with memory can resume a half-finished agent turn; a disk-only snapshot cannot. boxd, Lizard and Runtime capture memory by default. Sandboxer's stop snapshot captures memory, but its continuous and named snapshots are disk-only. Agent 37's fork copies the disk and boots fresh. InstaBox's homepage claims a fork copies running processes; its docs say a snapshot does not hold memory or processes, and fork is snapshot-save-plus-create.

A fork with memory is not free either. Runtime freezes the source while it writes memory, Lizard pauses it briefly, and boxd pauses it for a fraction of a second. None of them is a zero-impact clone of a busy machine.

concept.heading: What a restore does to what is there now
paragraphs: Two restore styles, and mixing them up loses work. In-place restore replaces what it finds: Agent 37's backup restore replaces the data rather than merging, and boxd's checkpoint restore is a reboot into the captured state that discards anything written afterwards. New-machine restore leaves the original alone: Sandboxer's named snapshots and Lizard's snapshots create a separate machine.

Retention is the other half. Boat keeps a stopped sandbox's disk for 14 days. Agent 37 keeps seven nightly backups. Sandboxer's storage quota is free but finite, and going over it blocks new sandboxes rather than charging.

comparisonIntro: Can you rewind, clone, or recover a machine — and does the copy include what was running?

rows.note: No snapshot product. Free nightly backups of `/home/node` (seven rotating slots) plus on-demand, restored in place only; a live fork copies the disk but not memory; templates are Dockerfile-built images.

source.quote: Every instance's data (`/home/node`) is backed up nightly into seven rotating slots

rows.note: Three snapshot kinds: a stop snapshot with disk and memory, continuous disk snapshots every ten minutes (two kept), and named disk snapshots used as templates with share codes. Forks are disk-only and boot fresh.

source.quote: Every 10 minutes while a sandbox runs, and at every stop

rows.note: A snapshot keeps memory and disk, is named and versioned, and boots new machines already running; a checkpoint is an in-place undo point (ten per machine); backups are disk-only and off-cluster; a fork copies memory and disk in 100–200 ms.

source.quote: A snapshot is a saved copy of a specific machine. It captures the disk and the memory

rows.note: Snapshots are disk-only and may stop the machine to take them; a fork is snapshot-save plus create, not an instant clone; snapshots survive deleting the machine and include saved logins.

source.quote: It is snapshot save plus create, so it takes about as long as those two.

rows.note: A snapshot captures memory, processes and the whole disk and restores into a new sandbox at the source's size; a fork copies a running sandbox 1–100 times with memory, pausing the source briefly. There is no trash.

source.quote: A snapshot saves a running sandbox's memory, running processes and every file on its disk.

rows.note: Snapshots default to memory plus disk, with disk-only opt-in; forks copy files, memory and processes but freeze the source while capturing; a sandbox with a volume cannot be snapshotted.

source.quote: Snapshots default to `mode: "memory"`. That mode keeps files, memory and running processes.

rows.note: Snapshots are automatic, disk-only and taken every minute, but only the newest one can be used: there is no point-in-time restore. Saved snapshots are named, never expire, and cost $0.056 a day beyond the included ten.

source.quote: Resume and fork always use the newest snapshot. You cannot go back to an older one.

questions: Does a snapshot include memory and running processes, or only files?
Can I boot several machines from one snapshot, and does the source keep running?
Is there a point-in-time restore, or only the newest snapshot?
Where is the copy stored — same host, same region, another provider?
Does restoring replace the disk or merge into it?
Do snapshots contain credentials, and who can restore them?
How long does a stopped machine's disk survive before it is deleted?

picks.situation: Undo a bad edit on one machine
picks.why: boxd has in-place checkpoints you can rewind to; Sandboxer takes a disk snapshot every ten minutes and keeps two. Most providers only offer a snapshot you remember to take.

picks.situation: Build a golden image and stamp out copies
picks.why: boxd's snapshot boots already running, Sandboxer's named snapshots work as templates with share codes, and Boat's saved snapshots never expire. Agent 37's closest equivalent is a Dockerfile-built template.
All three fork memory and processes. boxd's source pauses for a fraction of a second; Lizard and Runtime freeze it while memory is written, so the copy is not free of impact.

picks.situation: Disaster recovery if the host disappears
picks.why: boxd uploads disk backups to object storage off the cluster; Runtime copies snapshots off the server they came from. Agent 37's backups are folder-scoped and stored in the US.
Boat's saved snapshots never expire (beyond the included count), Sandboxer's named snapshots have no separate charge, and Lizard's snapshots persist while you have credit.

gotchas: Boat has no point-in-time restore: only the newest minute's snapshot is usable.
Agent 37's backup covers only `/home/node`, so a database installed in `/var/lib` is not in it.
Runtime cannot snapshot a sandbox with a volume attached.
InstaBox and Lizard snapshots carry credentials and saved logins.
boxd re-saving a snapshot name replaces the previous version and cleans up older ones.
Lizard's `stop` deletes the disk: only `/workspace` and snapshots survive, and there is no trash.
